editions.title: Nvidia's Huang out as CEO; Lutnick under fire
editions.notification: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off its value. Here is what it means for chips and Washington.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia's leadership upheaval. Co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and director with immediate effect, after admitting affairs with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security, and with Nvidia vice-president Kimberly Powell. Colette Kress is interim chief executive and Harvey Jones is the first independent chair. Shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, and the company has lost up to $601 billion of value. The first results without Huang are due on 17 November.

The scandal is widening into US policy. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entering the city-state, while saying US help in its Megaspeed probe was limited. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is reportedly under pressure from Congress and inside the White House after stalling export controls against Megaspeed, which CNN estimates bought more than $4bn of Nvidia chips. Commerce called reports of a clash with Treasury false. Trump has publicly backed Lutnick. Nvidia also privately told a lawmaker it could implement chip geotracking, which undercuts industry claims that such mandates are infeasible.

Beyond Nvidia, the day was dominated by fears for the AI trade. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% after Democrats' midterm gains raised the prospect of tougher AI and data-centre rules, wiping out over $2 trillion. Investors were not uniformly bearish: Nvidia largely recovered by Thursday's close, and Citi argued it is too early to call the AI trade structurally broken. OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though its losses widened, while Anthropic prepares its IPO next week.

top_stories.summary: Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entry and issued a stern warning, while finding insufficient evidence for offences. It said US authorities gave only limited help in the Supermicro-related probe. Singaporean buyers can account for over 20% of Nvidia's quarterly revenue.

top_stories.summary: Officials are reportedly discussing whether the Commerce Secretary should be fired after he failed to act on an intelligence report. Megaspeed was not added to the blacklist despite concerns, and Lutnick is due to testify before Congress. Commerce denies a clash with Treasury.

top_stories.summary: Axios reports Lutnick stalled US action against Megaspeed three times, prompting a challenge from Treasury. Trump reportedly told officials to proceed and has publicly backed Lutnick. The case sits at the heart of US-China chip export controls.

top_stories.summary: Republicans blamed Big Tech and data centres after Democratic wins, including in Mississippi and Ohio, where candidates campaigned against data-centre expansion. More than $2tn of market value was lost as investors feared a tougher AI regime in Congress.

top_stories.summary: Reported figures show OpenAI's quarterly revenue passed $10bn, but its adjusted operating loss grew to $10.9bn. Anthropic reportedly grew 47% to $17bn with a far smaller loss, ahead of its IPO next week. The numbers are unofficial and calculated differently.

editions.title: Jensen Huang quits Nvidia as CEO amid affair and China-spy scandal
editions.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off the chipmaker's value. Here's what it means.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker the most valuable in the world. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for China, and a second relationship with a direct report. Nvidia's shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, pushing market value below $4 trillion and erasing up to $601 billion, which would be the largest one-day loss for any stock if it held at the close.

The fallout is spreading into politics and markets. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports and on Huang's relationship, often a precursor to formal investigations. The New York Times reported that Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action, and the Wall Street Journal reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled action against Singapore-based Megaspeed, which may have funnelled chips to China. Trump has backed Lutnick publicly. Elsewhere, the tech sell-off hit broadly: the Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday after Democrats' midterm gains raised fears of AI regulation and data-centre curbs.

The bigger question is what comes next. Nvidia reports quarterly results on 17 November, its first without Huang, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded the stock this week. Anthropic's S-1 filing, which revealed rapid revenue growth and a claim that its models now run on AMD chips within days, adds pressure on Nvidia's software moat, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue. Investors will be watching the successor search and the governance fallout closely.

editions.title: Nvidia shares slide as reports of Jensen Huang's ouster mount
editions.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports say its board may move against CEO Jensen Huang. Here's what we know.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia. Its shares fell more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday and slid a further 7 to 8 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday, after the Wall Street Journal and New York Times reported that the board could meet as soon as the same day to decide the future of chief executive Jensen Huang. The reports follow Huang's admission of an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence agent, and a further alleged affair with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has hired former US attorney Joon H. Kim's firm to investigate, and US lawmakers have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Nvidia has not responded to comment requests, and the ouster reports remain unconfirmed rumours. Related chip stocks, including Korean memory makers and TSMC, are being watched for knock-on effects.

Elsewhere, the AI and chip economy kept generating deals. TSMC's board has reportedly approved up to $1 billion of investment in OpenAI and Anthropic, which would give the chipmaker direct stakes in two of its biggest customers, though analysts have flagged circular financing concerns. London chip designer Fractile raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, and South Korea's president said Samsung's packaging expansion could spur about $30 billion of further investment. Google DeepMind also unveiled AlphaProof Code, which formally verified the cryptographic core of Signal in four weeks.

On the consumer side, Google Wallet added digital home keys, Google Fi previewed a dual-carrier "super network", and reports suggest Grand Theft Auto VI has passed $1 billion in sales ahead of its 19 November release, a figure not yet confirmed by Take-Two. Regulators also acted: New York forced T-Mobile to drop data caps on low-income home internet plans, and Germany reportedly banned Chinese drones from military bases.

top_stories.summary: Nvidia fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading, erasing a small rebound, and has lost over 9.5 per cent across Monday and Tuesday. Media reports of a board meeting and further alleged affairs involving chief executive Jensen Huang have raised doubts about his job. As the leading AI chip maker, the leadership question matters for investors across the sector.

Lawmakers have also requested a closed-door briefing.

editions.title: Anthropic IPO talk builds as Nvidia's Huang faces FBI probe
editions.notification: Anthropic's IPO valuation talk climbs towards $1.5tn while Nvidia shares slide over the Huang probe.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is the twin pressure on Nvidia and the surge of talk around Anthropic. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn off its market value, after a class action accused the company and chief executive Jensen Huang of misleading shareholders over his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities reportedly concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia says it is running an independent investigation, and Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter. Related reports tie Alice Huang to more than $7bn of Nvidia chip sales to China, which could strengthen bipartisan calls to tighten chip export controls.

Anthropic dominated the AI news. The Financial Times reports the company is considering an IPO at up to $1.4tn, with bankers reportedly preparing to lift the target to $1.5tn or more, and Goldman Sachs projects revenue above $600bn by 2030. These are rumours and forecasts, not confirmed plans. The company also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in coding and research and lower prices, and expanded Claude into a workspace with spreadsheets, whiteboards and data tools.

Elsewhere, AMD detailed its Zen 6 core and its Venice-X and Verano server chips, Alibaba's T-Head filed for a Hong Kong IPO, and the FCC is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers that Microsoft is lobbying against. Regulation was also in focus, with a Paris Call on AI safety signed by ten AI companies but no deadlines or sanctions, and Australia recommending a new AI regulator after an OpenAI-linked breach.

top_stories.summary: Questions in Washington centre on possible exposure of sensitive information and Nvidia's China dealings, with calls for an independent investigation. The episode could add momentum to bipartisan efforts to tighten advanced chip controls on China.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang scandal wipes $190bn as AI sell-off lingers
editions.notification: Nvidia loses $190bn in a day as CEO Jensen Huang faces an investigation over a China-linked affair.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US officials reportedly concluded passed information to Chinese government channels. Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation, Congress has asked for a briefing by 11 November, and a class action alleges shareholders were misled. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn from its market value. Reports also suggest Moonshot AI accessed top Nvidia chips in China despite export curbs, which, if confirmed, would sharpen the debate over export controls.

Elsewhere, the AI sector is moving fast. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in speed and coding and lower prices, and reports say it is preparing a large IPO, with a valuation of up to $1.4tn. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon became generally available, and Meta launched a small, cheap model. Asian markets rebounded after a steep AI-led rout, while AMD forecast record revenue and said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time in a quarter.

Regulation and security also featured. Washington is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers, which Microsoft is lobbying against, and the UK may widen its under-16 social media ban to marketplaces such as Vinted and eBay. Binance was reported to have lost $6.3bn in what Bloomberg calls the largest crypto heist on record.

editions.title: Huang affair scandal rattles Nvidia as Anthropic readies IPO
editions.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang admits an affair as a probe into alleged Chinese spying begins. Shares slip.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is the scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has publicly apologised for an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly believes was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation and says it has no reason to believe sensitive information or national security was compromised. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, while broader US indices rose. Analysts say the affair could sharpen scrutiny of chip exports to China, and Congressional chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed, and the Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage claims.

The scandal sits alongside reports that point to the same underlying question: how China accesses advanced AI chips. Bloomberg reports that Moonshot AI used a large pool of Nvidia's top chips this summer, despite US export restrictions, and Wired reports Huang hired a crisis PR firm a year before he acknowledged the affair. Meanwhile AMD said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time in a single quarter, on AI accelerator demand.

In AI model news, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with prices cut to $8 and $40 per million input and output tokens. Bloomberg also reports Anthropic is planning a live-streamed IPO discussion between Dario Amodei and Jamie Dimon, though this is unconfirmed. Asian markets rebounded after a sharp AI-led sell-off, and Australia announced mandatory AI incident reporting after an OpenAI agent breach.

World.title: Putin rejects compromise as Nvidia shock and Iran tensions weigh
World.notification: Putin signals no compromise on Ukraine as Witkoff and Kushner leave Moscow empty-handed
World.summary:
Putin told US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow that Russia will not soften its terms on Ukraine, rejecting foreign peacekeepers and insisting on the four annexed regions. The talks followed Abu Dhabi meetings that produced a large prisoner exchange but no breakthrough, and Europe is pressing for a seat at the table. Putin's stance dampened hopes of a near-term deal, while a Ukrainian power grid under strain and new Starshield restrictions add pressure on Kyiv.

In the US, the week's biggest market story is Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has stepped down after admitting an affair, a second relationship has been reported, and the company has lost about $550bn in value in five days. Congress wants Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, and Lutnick is under fire over chip export curbs. Oil remains volatile: Brent rose to $93.82 as Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal, and two tankers were reportedly disabled in the Strait of Hormuz.

In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pursuing a reset with the EU ahead of a summit on 20 November, though Manchester United's sacking of Michael Carrick shows domestic turmoil too. Asia's focus is Xi's Taiwan remarks ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, and Indonesia's vice-president has resigned amid a fraying ruling alliance.

Tech.title: Nvidia in turmoil as Jensen Huang steps down
Tech.notification: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off its value. Here is what happens next.
Tech.summary:
Nvidia dominates today's tech news after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and longtime director Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows Huang's admission of an affair and reports linking one of the women involved, Alice Huang, to China's Ministry of State Security. Huang has denied any improper sharing of information with China. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, and at least seven Wall Street firms downgraded the stock this week.

The fallout is spreading. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entering the city-state, while saying US help in its probe into Megaspeed was limited. Senators Warren and Coons have asked the administration to preserve documents on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports suggest Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled action against Megaspeed, with officials discussing whether he should be fired. Lawmakers want Huang to appear at a closed-door hearing on 18 November, and the first quarterly results without him are due on 17 November.

Beyond Nvidia, the wider AI theme is mixed. Google and Samsung opened pre-orders for their Android XR smart glasses from $395, OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, and Republicans blamed data-centre backlash for midterm losses, which helped knock the Nasdaq down more than 5%.

Tech.title: Nvidia in turmoil as Jensen Huang steps down
Tech.notification: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off its value. Here is what happens next.
Tech.summary:
Nvidia dominates today's tech news after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and longtime director Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows Huang's admission of an affair and reports linking one of the women involved, Alice Huang, to China's Ministry of State Security. Huang has denied any improper sharing of information with China. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, and at least seven Wall Street firms downgraded the stock this week.

The fallout is spreading. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entering the city-state, while saying US help in its probe into Megaspeed was limited. Senators Warren and Coons have asked the administration to preserve documents on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports suggest Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled action against Megaspeed, with officials discussing whether he should be fired. Lawmakers want Huang to appear at a closed-door hearing on 18 November, and the first quarterly results without him are due on 17 November.

Beyond Nvidia, the wider AI theme is mixed. Google and Samsung opened pre-orders for their Android XR smart glasses from $395, OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, and Republicans blamed data-centre backlash for midterm losses, which helped knock the Nasdaq down more than 5%.

highlights.label: Succession
highlights.text: Harvey Jones is chair and Colette Kress is interim chief executive, with the FT framing their first task as steadying the company. Names floated for the permanent role include Lisa Su and Tim Cook.

highlights.label: Lutnick
highlights.text: Congress and reportedly the White House are pressing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed, with officials said to be discussing whether he should be fired.

highlights.label: OpenAI
highlights.text: OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue for the first time, though its operating loss widened. Anthropic reportedly grew revenue 47% ahead of its IPO next week.

highlights.label: Smart glasses
highlights.text: Google and Samsung's Intelligent Eyewear starts at $395 with no display and sales from 10 December, competing directly with Meta's Ray-Ban glasses.

highlights.label: Midterms and AI
highlights.text: The Nasdaq fell more than 5% as fears grew that a Democratic Congress would crack down on AI and data centres, wiping out over $2 trillion in value.

highlights.label: UK chips
highlights.text: London-based Fractile reportedly hit a $7bn valuation after a $720m Series C led by Thrive Capital, Lightspeed, Redpoint and Founders Fund.

points.text: Singapore bars alleged spy Alice Huang from re-entry and says US help in the Megaspeed probe was limited.

Gemini is rolling out to Apple CarPlay worldwide, adding hands-free Gemini Live to the in-car AI assistant race.
Tech stocks rebounded on Wednesday as the Nasdaq erased last week's losses, with the Stoxx 600 closing at a record.
UK AI infrastructure start-up Nscale is reportedly weighing a delay to its roughly $35bn IPO amid the tech sell-off.

World.title: Putin rejects compromise as Nvidia shock and Iran tensions weigh
World.notification: Putin signals no compromise on Ukraine as Witkoff and Kushner leave Moscow empty-handed
World.summary:
Putin told US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow that Russia will not soften its terms on Ukraine, rejecting foreign peacekeepers and insisting on the four annexed regions. The talks followed Abu Dhabi meetings that produced a large prisoner exchange but no breakthrough, and Europe is pressing for a seat at the table. Putin's stance dampened hopes of a near-term deal, while a Ukrainian power grid under strain and new Starshield restrictions add pressure on Kyiv.

In the US, the week's biggest market story is Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has stepped down after admitting an affair, a second relationship has been reported, and the company has lost about $550bn in value in five days. Congress wants Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, and Lutnick is under fire over chip export curbs. Oil remains volatile: Brent rose to $93.82 as Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal, and two tankers were reportedly disabled in the Strait of Hormuz.

In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pursuing a reset with the EU ahead of a summit on 20 November, though Manchester United's sacking of Michael Carrick shows domestic turmoil too. Asia's focus is Xi's Taiwan remarks ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, and Indonesia's vice-president has resigned amid a fraying ruling alliance.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down amid an affair scandal, wiping about $550bn off the company. Congress wants testimony from Huang and Lutnick.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: Burnham says a 'win-win' EU deal could be done, with food, emissions and youth mobility deals targeted before the 20 November summit.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Zelenskyy wants the EU to be a regular part of Ukraine talks, while leaders remain split over who should represent the bloc.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Xi said Taiwan's reunification 'will certainly be realised' but made no mention of force, a week before the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrat Scott Colom unseated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, part of a wider Democratic Senate gain.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned after a court ruling on his campaign documents, exposing a rift in the ruling alliance.

points.text: Brent crude rose to $93.82 after Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal; the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to about 5.07%.
The IRGC says two supertankers were disabled by explosions in Hormuz, a chokepoint for about a fifth of global oil.
Iran threatened US bases in Europe as US prosecutors charged three men over attacks claimed by a group that hit seven targets in Britain.
Manchester United sacked head coach Michael Carrick, leaving the club 18th in the Premier League; Mauricio Pochettino is reportedly the target.
The EU is set to delay a 10% tariff on UK-made electric cars, though the UK car industry wants a two-year delay rather than one.
An Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital killed at least six people as progress on Trump's Gaza Peace Plan stalled.

Fashion.title: Capri names new CEO as Idol steps back; luxury leadership shuffles
Fashion.notification: Capri appoints Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive, as John Idol retires.
Fashion.summary:
Capri Holdings, owner of Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo, has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long tenure. Idol stays on as a senior adviser until March, and Robin Freestone becomes independent chairman. The change comes as fiscal second-quarter sales fell 5.5%, although margins improved and earnings beat expectations. Sources also say Capri has been talking to potential acquirers about a sale.

Leadership is shifting across the sector more broadly. Tod's is losing creative director Matteo Tamburini after nearly three years, with no successor named, while Hugo Boss CEO Daniel Grieder steps down at the end of 2026 and David Epstein from Frasers Group takes over in January 2027, following Frasers' 50.08% stake. Burberry's Daniel Lee, Pal Zileri's new creative director Norbert Stumpfl and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands reshaping their teams and strategies.

Demand remains the underlying worry. PwC says 70% of surveyed consumers have given up buying luxury over value concerns, Gulf shoppers are cutting back amid war-linked inflation, and groups are looking to the US as China stalls. Brands are responding with cheaper entry products and price cuts.

highlights.label: Tod's
highlights.text: Creative director Matteo Tamburini is leaving after nearly three years, with no successor named. The brand is refocusing on Italian craftsmanship.

highlights.label: Hugo Boss
highlights.text: CEO Daniel Grieder steps down on 31 December. David Epstein of Frasers takes over, as the group becomes a Frasers subsidiary.

highlights.label: Demand
highlights.text: A PwC study finds 70% of consumers have stopped buying luxury over value concerns. Dior, Chanel and Gucci are responding with lower-priced lines and cuts.

highlights.label: Gulf and China
highlights.text: Gulf shoppers are cutting luxury spending as war inflation bites, and groups are turning to the US as Chinese growth stalls.

highlights.label: Burberry
highlights.text: Daniel Lee's Vogue profile points to a move towards more wearable collections and a turnaround, with pretax profit reported above $65m in 2026.

highlights.label: Collaborations
highlights.text: Balenciaga and Damien Hirst release Damienciaga to mark the Le City bag's 25th, and Rimowa teams up with Maison Margiela.
